Each congregation buries its own, and the sexton keeps the roll that inheritance disputes are settled from. Guilds buy plots together so their members lie among their trade.
A community of the religious. Sometimes runs a hospital or school.
An order living in common. It may keep a hospital or a school.
Tends the sick poor. Generally in religious hands.
The ailing poor are nursed here, most often by a religious order.

A charity house sheltering the destitute poor, the aged, and the disabled who cannot work. Church endowment and wealthy donors pay for it. Board and lodging are given; prayers for the benefactors are returned.

Kept for the poor, the old, and the crippled who have no work in them, funded by church endowment and rich patrons. It feeds and houses its residents, who repay the kindness in prayer for those who gave it.

Takes in abandoned infants and small children and keeps them in basic care until they are apprenticed, placed with families, or raised on within its walls. The church usually runs it. A turning wheel set in the wall lets a child be left anonymously after dark.

Abandoned babies and young children are received here and given plain care until apprenticeship, a family placement, or a childhood spent in the house itself. Generally a church foundation. The wheel in the wall admits a child by night, no name asked.

Senior druids who govern how their circle deals with the town. They may keep a grove hidden beneath the streets, hold the line between the town's spread and the wild, or advise its rulers on the land.

A council of elder druids charged with their circle's standing in the town: sometimes tending a concealed grove below the streets, sometimes mediating between expansion and wild ground, sometimes counselling those in power on ecological matters.
One of the lord's choosing governs, and noble authority overrides whatever the town was accustomed to.
Rule falls to the lord's appointee, whose noble warrant stands above local custom.
A loose council of leading citizens sees to the town's common business. It answers to no one in particular, but the work gets done.
The town's notables gather and settle its common business by consensus. Less answerable than an elected body, but steady.
The town's leadership, whether elected or named to office.
A mayor and council, come to office by vote or appointment.
The guilds hold the town's politics, their masters seated on the council.
Town rule belongs to the guilds; it is the guildmasters who fill the council's chairs.
Civic power belongs solely to the wealthy merchant families, and office is bought in all but name.
A handful of rich merchant houses monopolise power here; a political post is, in practice, something one purchases.
The official voice, reading proclamations, market prices, and news at set hours in the market square. Town or guild pays the wage.
At fixed times the proclamations, the prices, and the news are called out in the market square. The town pays for it, or else a guild.
Buildings of several storeys, in timber and stone.
Timber and stone, raised to more than one floor.
Water from wells, fountains, or pipe.
Wells and fountains, or water carried in by pipe.
Where the town meets and its business is done.
The seat of assembly and administration.
The borough's court, where local justice is done.
A borough court for the settling of local matters.
Cells to hold prisoners, and stocks to shame them.
A few cells, and a place for punishment in public view.

The able-bodied poor are given shelter and food, and made to earn it at compulsory labour: textile work, grinding, construction. It is not a prison, though the distinction is thin. It thins the ranks of vagrants and turns out goods besides, and its conditions are kept harsh on purpose, so that none grow too content to leave.

In return for a roof and a meal, the able-bodied poor are set to forced work: textiles, milling, construction. Not quite a gaol, but the line blurs. It cuts vagrancy and yields product, and the deliberately grim conditions are the point: dependency is meant to sting.
Gated stone defences. Costly to raise and no cheaper to keep up.
Masonry walls pierced by gates. Dear to build, dearer to maintain.
Guarded ways in and out, each with its keeper.
Entry controlled at fixed points, gatekeepers posted.
Part-time guards who walk the night and hold the gates.
Watchmen serving part-time. Night patrols and gate duty.
Quarters for the guard or a small garrison.
Lodging for guardsmen, or a modest garrison.
The inner fortress, and the last refuge when a siege closes in.
An innermost stronghold, the city's final hold under siege.

A billet and hiring office for professional soldiers idle between campaigns. Caravan escort, garrison work, and short-term hire go at day-wages here. Cheaper than a standing army and steadier than a mob. These are salaried men who fight in formation, not for plunder.

Where a band of soldiers lodges and takes contracts between wars. They hire out by the day for escort, garrison duty, and brief campaigns: less costly than keeping an army, more dependable than a rabble. They form up for a wage, not for treasure.
A ranger post. Those here watch the wilds, keep the trails, and follow the movements of beasts. In a crisis they turn scout and tracker.
Rangers keep this lodge, minding the wilderness about the town, tending its trails, and marking where the beasts migrate. When trouble comes they scout and track for the town.
A single wizard's residence.
A body of spellcasters organised together.
An association of magic-workers.
Sells spell scrolls. A minor charm costs a craftsman a month's earnings; a greater working, a merchant's year.
Scrolls of spells across the counter: the smallest charm at a craftsman's month of pay, a greater working at a merchant's year.
A permanent circle, and a rare one. Dear to build and dearer to keep, calling for magical skill past what a town usually commands.
Rarely seen: a fixed teleportation circle whose construction and upkeep cost enormously, and which demands expertise beyond the ordinary town's means.
A chartered hall that serves as the region's chief adventuring hub. It posts contracts, grades the monster threats, keeps gear in repair, and runs the large operations no militia could handle.

The region's principal adventuring hub, working under charter. Contracts are posted here, monster threats graded, equipment maintained, and the great operations beyond any militia coordinated from its floor.
A board where torchbearers and porters sign on by the session at a day labourer's wage.
Torchbearers and porters take work here by the session, paid what a day labourer earns.
Professional fighters, alone or in small bands, taking private work: guarding a person, collecting a debt, or quietly ending a difficulty.
Fighters for private hire, singly or in small groups: bodyguarding, debt-collection, and the discreet removal of problems.
Contraband moved, and the duty on it never paid.
Trade in forbidden goods, kept off the tax rolls.
Pickpockets and bruisers working together. Ten to thirty strong.
An organised crew of cutpurses and toughs, some 10 to 30 of them.
Honest-looking trades that mask the dishonest kind.
Lawful businesses standing cover for unlawful work.
Tunnels and false cellars, dug and linked to move contraband beneath the streets.
A network of excavated passages joining cellars and yards to the town's edge. None of it on any map.
Message birds kept above a city yard by people who declare nothing. The word arrives unsigned and moves faster than the watch.
An undeclared loft in the roofs. Unsigned messages in and out, protected by whichever organization currently holds the street.
Bards, jugglers, and acrobats, come for the festivals.
The festivals bring bards, jugglers, and acrobats through.
Fixed houses for performance.
Standing venues for the stage.
Dice, cards, and the plainer games of chance.
Games of chance: dice and cards, nothing elaborate.
Prostitution, tolerated or licensed.
A house of prostitution, suffered or regulated.
Combat outside the law, or barely within it, held underground.
Fights unlawful or half-lawful, staged in hidden places.
Trains fighters for the crowd's amusement, drawn from prisoners, debtors, and volunteers. It supplies the arena circuit.
Prisoners, debtors, and the willing are made into fighters for public show, and sent on to feed the arenas.
'Divination' with no magic in it, done by Deception, a few coins a reading.
Fortunes told by Deception, with no real magic in them, for a few coins each.
Fur processors, traders, and retailers gathered into one quarter. It is high-value work, for good fur is a luxury good.
Those who dress, trade, and sell fur, all pressed into one district. The trade runs high, quality pelts being luxuries.
Trade that never closes, spread across several sites.
Standing markets in more than one quarter, open every day.
Several standing market squares, one to a district.
Permanent markets in more than one square, each serving its own quarter.
Merchants from abroad. Letters of credit are honoured.
Foreign traders attend, and credit by letter is taken.
Much of the city's trade is in their hands.
Between them they handle much of the city's trade.
Loans, coin exchange, and letters of credit. The beginnings of banking.
Lending, currency exchange, and credit by letter. Rudimentary banking.
Several inn districts, given over to merchants, travellers, and those who stay long.
More than one quarter of inns, serving the merchant, the traveller, and the lingering guest.

Permanent offices where caravan masters, merchants, and armed escorts do business. It handles bonded freight, route intelligence, the assembly of armed convoys, and the settling of commercial disputes.

A city-scale exchange with standing offices, where caravan masters meet merchants and armed escorts to transact. Bonded freight, route intelligence, armed convoy assembly, and commercial dispute resolution are all conducted here.
A city-scale yard building large merchant ships and warships alike. It holds several dry docks, a ropewalk, a sail loft, and its own ironworks. It employs many, and matters to the state's defence.
Here large merchant and war vessels are built at city scale, across multiple dry docks, with ropewalk, sail loft, and dedicated ironworks besides. A major employer, and a strategic military asset.
Where there is coast or river to reach. Bulk trade cannot do without them.
Present only with sea or river access, and indispensable to trade in bulk.
Several large grain stores feed the city between them. The state keeps them.
Grain held in large state-run stores and given out across the city.
Where merchant goods are stored.
Storage set aside for the merchants' stock.
Heated communal baths. Some cultures make them a social hub, others suspect them of vice; either way they are the district's best place for rumour and news.
A public bathhouse with hot water, a gathering place in some cultures and a suspected den of vice in others. Nowhere in the district hears more news.
A settled auction block with holding pens, registered brokers, and papers of provenance. Commerce in persons, sanctioned by law, taxed and regulated and woven into the city's economy.
An established block for the sale of persons, with holding facilities, licensed brokers, and provenance documents. The law permits it; it is taxed, regulated, and set deep in the city economy.

A standing, licensed quarter for the trade in persons: auction halls, holding compounds, broker offices, and the legal and financial apparatus around them. It works at a scale no single market block could reach.

A permanent district, licensed for commerce in persons, with auction halls, holding compounds, broker offices, and the attendant legal and financial infrastructure. The scale runs well beyond one market block.
Tests precious metal brought to market for purity, charging by the assay. Banking and minting depend on it.
An office that assays the purity of gold and silver brought to market, for a fee each time. Minting and banking cannot work without it.
Coin struck under state or noble charter. It sets a single standard of currency across the region and returns a steady revenue through seigniorage.
Chartered by state or noble to make coin, it standardises the region's currency and yields significant ongoing revenue by seigniorage.

A guild house of the listening trade. Correspondents kept on several roads, an archive that sets one report against another, and a fixed price for an answer in writing. Costly, and the only counter that grades a claim before selling it.
A chartered house of correspondents. Reports arrive from several roads and are checked against each other before anything is sold. The written answer carries a standing rate and a grade.
Wheels turn on every usable stream, many licensed by guild or city.
Every workable watercourse turns a wheel, most under a guild's or the city's licence.
General forges, farriers, and toolsmiths in each quarter.
Every quarter has its forges: farriers, toolsmiths, and general smiths.
Armourers, swordsmiths, and jewellers, each in its own guild.
Swordsmiths, armourers, jewellers. The trades kept to separate guilds.
Silks, spices, and other precious goods.
The trade in silk, spice, and precious things.
Guild-organised carpenters, joiners, and furniture makers for building and fitting out.
Builders' carpenters, joiners, and furniture makers, each trade organised under its guild.

Apothecary shops crowded into one quarter, where competition forces each to specialise. One leans to chirurgery, another to herbal preparations, a third to imported medicines. Between them they carry herbalism kits, medicinal herbs, surgical supplies, and basic antidotes.

A cluster of apothecaries pressed close enough that competition drives them apart in trade, some to surgery, some to herb-work, some to medicines brought from abroad. Herbalism kits, medicinal herbs, surgical supplies, and basic antidotes are all to be had.
Guild bowyers and fletchers selling arrows by the sheaf, special broadheads, and composite bows to order, supplying the watch, the garrison, and the caravans.
Arrows by the sheaf, specialty broadheads, and commissioned composite bows from the guild's bowyers and fletchers. The watch, the garrison, and the caravans buy here.
Planks and beams for the building trade, sawn by water or ox power at a mill with a permanent crew.
A mill turned by water or oxen that saws planks and beams for construction and keeps a standing crew.
Brews ale and beer at commercial scale for the taverns and for regional sale. A major employer and a heavy buyer of grain.
Commercial brewing of ale and beer supplies the taverns and ships across the region, employing many and consuming grain in bulk.
Meat markets and shambles kept under strict civic rules.
The shambles and meat markets, closely regulated by the city.
Every ward has its bakehouses, with weights and prices set by the guild.
Bakehouses throughout the wards, the loaf's weight and price fixed by guild rule.
Windows, vessels, and mirrors. The craft demands real skill.
Glass for windows, vessels, and mirrors. Expert work, not casual.

A guild of professional cartographers turning out regional maps, sea charts, property surveys, and military reconnaissance. It sells ready-made maps and works to commission. No maps in the region are more accurate than the city's.

Professional cartographers, guild-organised, producing regional maps, sea charts, property surveys, and reconnaissance maps for the army. Some sell off the shelf, others are drawn to order. The city's are the most accurate maps the region has.
Specialisation carried to an extreme, down to gold-beaters and mirror-makers.
Trades split so finely they yield gold-beaters and mirror-makers.
Several alchemical workshops, run under a guild.
A cluster of alchemists' workshops, organised into a guild.
A house of worship to every quarter.
One for each neighbourhood.
The grounds inside the walls filled generations back, so the dead are lifted when their term is up and their bones stacked to make room. New ground lies outside the gates.
Carts go out at dusk to ground bought beyond the walls, and the charnel house holds what the old plots gave up. What a family endowed decides who is lifted and who is left.
Several houses, each of a different order.
More than one monastery, and no two of the same order.
The bishop's seat, and its presence marks a city as a major one.
Seat of a bishop, and the mark of a first-rank city.
A large house for the sick poor, of 50 to 100 beds.
Fifty to a hundred beds, given over to the ailing poor.
A governor appointed by king or duke holds sway, and the city runs as a noble fief.
Rule falls to a royal or ducal appointee, the city being worked as a noble's fief.
Officials, clerks, and ward officers do the city's daily business between them, whoever gives the orders. It runs by the momentum of its own paperwork.
A standing body of officials, clerks, and ward officers carries out the city's administration, functional whatever rules above it. What moves it is bureaucratic inertia.
A civic council backed by a complete administrative staff.
A civic council with the full apparatus of office beneath it.
Effective power over the city sits with a consortium of guild masters.
The guild masters, banded into a consortium, hold the real civic power.
The settlement rules itself and the land around it as a sovereign polity, answering to no higher lord and holding no external charter.
An independent state in its own right, governing both itself and its hinterland. No overlord above it, no charter granted from outside.
Formal power rests with an assembly of citizens; those entitled to vote argue and decide the major ordinances and appointments.
A citizens' assembly wields the formal authority, its eligible voters debating and settling the larger ordinances and the appointments to office.
The crown governs the city from here, in person or through a royal governor. The standing is high, and so is the scrutiny.
The crown governs here at first hand, whether the monarch sits in it or a viceroy does. Great prestige, and no less watchfulness.
The official announcer, reading proclamations, market prices, and news in the market squares at set hours, paid by the city or a guild.
Employed by the city or a guild to call proclamations, prices, and news in the market squares at fixed times.
Buildings of several storeys. Tenements house the poor.
Multi-storey construction, with tenements for the poor.
A built water supply: conduits, cisterns, and fountains.
Engineered waterworks: conduits feeding cisterns and fountains.
A commanding seat of civic government.
An imposing hall for the city's affairs.
Separate courts for trade, for crime, and for the church.
Commercial, criminal, and ecclesiastical benches, each in its own house.
Holds debtors, criminals, and political prisoners alike.
For debtors, for criminals, and for the politically inconvenient.
Drains laid underground. Uncommon, and vital to public health.
Buried drainage. A rarity, and one the city's health depends on.
Towered stone walls. Several gatehouses along their length.
Masonry ramparts studded with towers and pierced by many gates.
A standing force of the law, roughly one in a hundred residents.
Full-time keepers of order, about one for every hundred people in the city.
A professional force, kept under arms for pay.
A standing force, paid to bear arms.
Sellsword companies under proper organisation, mustering hundreds to thousands.
Organised bands of hired blades. Major forces, hundreds to thousands strong.
Home to a powerful spellcaster. A city may hold more than one.
The seat of a high-level mage. Several may stand in a single city.
Magic items made to order.
Where magic items are crafted.
A permanent teleportation circle. Its use is restricted and its upkeep dear, but any settlement fortunate enough to hold one is transformed by it.
A fixed teleportation circle, guarded in its access and costly to keep. For the rare settlement that has one, it changes everything.
Guilds set against one another.
Specialised kit for the delving trade. Warded weapons, silver weapons, and the like.
Gear for those who go underground. Warded weapons, silver weapons, and such.
Scholars and researchers, gathered in number.
A cluster of learned men and their researches.
An organised trade in contraband.
Contraband, moved by an organised hand.
Rival gangs, forever disputing their turf.
Several gangs at odds, quarrelling over ground.
A chapter of organised crime. Thirty to a hundred members.
An arm of the wider criminal order, 30 to 100 strong.
Warehouses, taverns, and shops that mask criminal work.
Criminal operations screened behind honest-looking warehouses, taverns, and shops.

Multiple smiths with specializations.

Works precious metals and gemstones into rings, necklaces, seals, and luxury items. Accepts commissions, appraises stones, and occasionally buys stolen goods from discreet customers.
At city scale jewellers sit inside the specialized metalworkers' guilds (their row names them).
Silks, spices, precious goods.
Construction carpenters, joiners, and furniture makers, organised by guild.
Builds/repairs buildings and tools.
Builds houses, carts, furniture.
Construction and furniture makers.
Roof repair and construction.
Towns roof in tile and slate, and many forbid thatch for fear of fire.
Makes barrels for storage and transport.

Multiple apothecary shops clustered together. Competition drives specialization. Some focus on chirurgery, others on herbal preparations, others on imported medicines. Herbalism kits, medicinal herbs, surgical supplies, and basic antidotes all available.
Sells herbal medicines, poultices, and common remedies. No magical compounds, no acid flasks. Knows which roots treat fever and which mushrooms kill. Stocked with herbalism supplies.

A proper shop with a trained herbalist, stocked inventory, and a back room for consultations. Sells herbalism kit supplies, common antidotes, medicinal herbs, and basic surgical dressings. Some double as chirurgeons.
Guild bowyers and fletchers: standard arrows by the sheaf, specialty broadheads, composite bows to commission. Supplies the watch, the garrison, and the caravans.
Makes bows, crossbows, and arrows. Sells finished ammunition and takes custom bow commissions. The first stop for any adventurer whose quiver is empty.
Multiple craftsmen organized under a guild. Standard arrows by the sheaf, specialty broadheads, composite bows to commission. Restocks merchant caravans and outfits their guards.
A water- or ox-powered mill producing planks and beams for the construction trade. Employs a permanent crew.
Water- or ox-powered saw. Converts raw logs to planks and beams whenever logs can be had, for building and furniture.
A water- or ox-powered mill producing planks and beams for the construction trade. A town near timber can supply an entire region's building needs. Employs a permanent crew.
Commercial-scale ale and beer production supplying taverns and regional distribution. Major grain consumer and employer.
Converts malted grain to ale in quantity. The largest consumer of grain after bread. Supplies alehouses and households.
Commercial-scale ale and beer production. Supplies the town's taverns and regional distribution. Major grain consumer and employer.
Presses and ages wine from local grapes or imported must, in any year that either reaches the cellar. What it makes is sold in bulk, and by the bottle to wealthy clients.
Leather production. Foul-smelling; sited by water and toward the settlement edge where the ground allows.
Converts hides into leather using oak bark, whenever hides can be had. Foul-smelling. Placed downstream. Essential for shoes, harness, and straps.
Full-scale tannery with multiple vats and a guild-trained workforce. Produces high-quality leather for shoes, armour, and saddlery.
Finishes woven cloth by cleaning and thickening it. Often water-powered. Transforms raw weave into durable textile.
Applies colour to raw or woven cloth. Essential for producing anything beyond undyed grey wool.
Cloth production. Often guild-organized.
A wheel and a small kiln for domestic pottery: plates, jugs, storage vessels, made whenever clay can be had.
Moulds and fires clay bricks for construction whenever clay can be had. Enables more permanent buildings. Requires clay and fuel.
Organised shoemakers producing boots, shoes, and sandals for the urban population. Strictly regulated quality.
Makes and repairs shoes and boots. Every person needs footwear. One of the most reliable and consistent trades.
Master clothiers producing garments from finished cloth. Produces everything from working clothes to livery.
Cuts and sews finished cloth into garments. Serves the middling sort between home seamstress and master clothier.
Shambles and meat markets under strict civic regulation.
Meat processing. Strictly regulated.
Bakehouses in every ward. Guild-regulated weights and prices.
Bread production. Guild-regulated prices.
Converts raw ore to refined metal using charcoal-fueled furnaces, whenever ore can be had.
Makes candles from tallow and beeswax. Also produces soap and rope from similar raw materials. Essential for lighting.
Windows, vessels, mirrors. Requires expertise.
Small-scale glasswork, when sand can be had: bottles, window panes, goblets. Requires silica sand, potash, and a skilled furnace operator.
Twists fibres (hemp, flax, or plant matter) into rope and cordage. Essential for ships, construction, and agriculture.
Assists with births, manages difficult labours, and provides basic gynecological care. The most-used medical service in any settlement.
Carves functional and decorative items from wood: tool handles, religious figures, furniture inlays. Produces sacred images and reliquaries for the church.
Can read and write. Copies letters, draws up simple contracts, reads documents for the illiterate. Often the priest's assistant or a monastery-educated lay person.
Town record-keeping sits with guild clerks and the crier; the printing house is the city's writing trade.

A guild of professional cartographers producing regional maps, sea charts, property surveys, and military reconnaissance maps. Sells off-the-shelf maps and takes commissions. The city's maps are the most accurate in the region.
A craftsman who draws and sells maps: regional road maps, property surveys, and rough wilderness sketches from traveler accounts. Rare enough that most villages don't have one.

Sells road maps, regional surveys, and coastal charts. Takes commissions for estate surveys and dungeon sketching. Maintains a reference collection of older maps for consultation. Standard stop for adventurers, merchants, and military scouts.
the senior craft-guild master
Regulate quality, prices, and apprenticeships.
Extreme specialization (gold-beaters, mirror-makers).
Over a hundred distinct craft specializations. A guild for every conceivable trade.
Multiple alchemical workshops. Guild organization.
Potions and alchemical wares. A basic healing draught costs about what a labourer earns in a week.
Simple prayer marker. No resident clergy.
Simple prayer location. No clergy.
A roadside prayer marker at the parish edge. No clergy of its own.
Inside a town every street is in reach of a parish church.
Access to parish church
A walk of a few miles to the village house of worship for services.
Services mean the walk to the village house of worship, usually a few miles off.
Center of village life. Stone construction. Mandatory tithes.
Several houses of worship within town.
Scores of parishes, from fifty to a hundred and more. The faith reaches every street of the city.

A corner of the holding left out of the plough, banked with turf and marked with fieldstones. No clergy lives near enough to speak over anyone, so the words are said by whoever knew the dead best. The oldest markers have lost their names to the weather and are kept clear anyway.

A walled plot at the edge of the settlement, gated against livestock and kept by the households in turn. The rite is held when a priest comes through, and the burial itself does not wait for one. Families lie in rows by household, whatever their standing. That is the custom here, and has nothing to do with being poor.

Consecrated ground beside the house of worship, on its own plot, with a resident priest to close it. The rite is held on the day of the death, with no wait for a travelling clergyman, and the congregation has begun keeping the names in the same book as the births. The ground nearest the wall is spoken for generations ahead, and everyone here can say who holds it.

Each congregation keeps its own burial ground, and one that has filled its ground buries beyond the town's edge instead. The sexton holds the register of who lies where, which is the town's longest unbroken record and the one it reaches for in an inheritance dispute. Guilds buy plots together so their members lie among their trade.
Burial grounds and charnel house

The old grounds inside the walls filled generations ago, so the dead are lifted once their term is up and their bones stacked in the charnel house to make room for the next. New ground has been bought outside the gates, and the carts that go out at dusk are a fixed part of the city's evening. Who is lifted and who is left where they lie is settled by what a family endowed.

Burial has left the walls entirely: grounds beyond every gate, each with its own road, its own gatekeepers, and a trade in plots that the revenue office watches. The local registers are copied into a central roll because no single ground can any longer say where its own dead are. Wards are assigned to grounds, so a family that moves across the city can find itself divided by the assignment.
Performs sacraments, collects tithes. Often only literate person.
At town scale the clergy are held inside the parish churches' row.
Religious community. May operate hospital/school.
Five to ten major monastic houses: scholarly, contemplative, and charitable functions at scale.
Bishop's seat. Defines major city status.
Metropolitan cathedral. Seat of the highest regional religious authority. Pilgrimage destination.
Care for sick poor. Usually religious-run.
Large facility for sick poor. 50-100 beds.
Multiple hospitals and infirmaries across districts. Organized medical care at population scale.

Charitable house for the destitute poor, aged, and disabled who cannot work. Funded by church endowment and wealthy donors. Residents receive food and shelter; in return they pray for their benefactors.

Receives abandoned infants and young children, providing basic care until they can be apprenticed, placed with families, or raised within the institution. Usually church-run. The wheel in the wall allows anonymous deposit at night.

A circle of druids tied to the land. They regulate the seasons, mediate disputes with wild creatures, and know which streams run clean. More common in forested or isolated settlements, but they adapt. Some circles tend city gardens or hidden urban groves.
In towns and cities the druids speak through the Elder Grove Council.

A council of senior druids who govern their circle's relationship with the settlement around it. They may maintain a hidden grove beneath the streets, mediate between the settlement's growth and wild places, or serve as ecological advisors to the ruling authority.
The eldest or most respected farmer guides communal decisions by consensus.
A free hamlet with no lord's representative. Communal elder consensus governs shared affairs.
The village elders decide shared affairs together. No reeve, no steward: the old families settle it among themselves.
A town governs through a council or an appointee.
All family heads hold equal voice on shared concerns. Slower but more egalitarian.
Only a handful of households can all sit at one table.
A steward appointed by a distant lord to oversee the settlement. Authority is formal but often resented.
Larger holdings get a lord's steward.
One household head acts as de facto voice for the settlement. No formal appointment, no title. Just the person everyone goes to when something needs deciding.
A single household head speaks for a thorp; larger places need a headman or elders.
A royal or ducal appointee governs; the city operates as a noble fief.
A lord's agent manages the hamlet's lands, collects rents, and enforces noble authority.
A lord's steward collects rents and enforces manor authority over a bound village.
A lord's appointed official governs; noble authority supersedes local custom.
A single respected figure acts as de facto authority. Not elected, not appointed, simply acknowledged. Decisions are practical, made without ceremony.
A town governs through a council or an appointee.
An administrative apparatus of officials, clerks, and ward officers carries out the city's business, whoever sits above it. Functional, and moved by bureaucratic inertia.
Elected from the peasantry. Organises labour obligations, mediates disputes, and represents the village to outside authority.
A council of prominent citizens sees to the town's common affairs. Less accountable than an elected council, but steady.
The oldest or most respected resident guides village decisions on the strength of standing alone; no office goes with it.
A town governs through a council or an appointee.
Civic council with full administrative apparatus.
Elected or appointed town leadership.
A consortium of guild masters holds effective civic power.
Guilds control town politics. The guildmasters sit on the council.
Wealthy merchant families hold exclusive civic power; political office is effectively purchased.
The settlement governs itself and its surrounding territory as an independent polity. No higher lord, no external charter.
the speaker of the assembly
A citizen assembly holds formal authority; eligible voters debate and vote on major ordinances and appointments.
The crown's own seat of government, held by the monarch or by a governor in the crown's name. High status, high scrutiny.
Official announcer who reads proclamations, market prices, and news at fixed times in the market squares. Employed by the city or a guild.
Official announcer who reads proclamations, market prices, and news at fixed times in the market square. Employed by the town or a guild.
Wattle-and-daub or timber. 1-2 rooms per household.
Timber-frame with thatched roofs.
Timber construction with stone foundations.
Multi-story timber and stone buildings.
Multi-story buildings. Tenements for poor.
Dense multi-story blocks, tenement courts, and suburbs spilling past the walls.
Well or spring. At least a bucketful a person each day.
Well or spring access.
Wells and springs throughout village.
Wells, fountains, or piped water.
Aqueduct or water system
Engineered water supply. Conduits, cisterns, fountains.
Multiple aqueducts, cisterns, and distributed fountains. City-wide water management at scale.
Meeting place and administrative center.
Seat of metropolitan or state government: palace, ministries, audience halls, administrative bureaux.
Borough court for local justice.
Commercial, criminal, and ecclesiastical courts.
Specialized courts (commercial, criminal, appellate, ecclesiastical) operating simultaneously.
Holding cells and public punishment.
Debtors, criminals, political prisoners.
State prison complex: political prisoners, debtors, convicted criminals held separately.

The able-bodied poor receive shelter and food in exchange for compulsory labour: textile work, grinding, construction. Not a prison but the line is blurry. Reduces vagrancy and produces goods. Conditions are deliberately harsh to discourage dependency.
Underground drainage. Rare but critical for health.
Largest repository of knowledge in the region: thousands of volumes, map archives, historical records.
Sharpened stakes encircling the settlement. Offers minimal protection but enough to deter casual raiders.
Basic wooden palisade or earthwork berm. Slows raids and creature incursions.
Perimeter palisade or earthwork berm. Controls approach, slows attackers.
Stone fortifications with gates. Expensive to build and maintain.
City walls and gates
Masonry walls with towers. Multiple gatehouses.
Massive walls and fortifications
Layered wall systems: an outer wall and an inner wall, with gatehouses along both.
Controlled entry points with gatekeepers.
City walls carry their gates in their own row.
Full-time law enforcement. About one officer for every hundred people.
One able-bodied adult from each household musters with hunting bows, spears, and farm tools when danger reaches the fields.
Able-bodied residents drill and muster against local threats. Part-time service.
Organised community defense. Musters for raids and monster incursions. More reliable than hamlet levies.
Part-time guards. Night patrol and gate duty.
Householders who take turns walking the lanes after dark, keep a lantern at the crossroads, and raise the alarm. Unpaid; the rota is their own.
Housing for guards or small garrison.
A professional force, under arms full-time.
Garrison forces distributed across quarters. No single barracks can secure a metropolis.
Inner fortress. Last refuge in siege.
Organized sellsword companies. Major forces (hundreds to thousands).

A billet and contracting office for a band of professional soldiers available between campaigns. Offers caravan escort, garrison contracts, and short-term military hire at day-wage rates. Cheaper than a standing army, more reliable than a mob. These men fight in formation on salary, not for treasure.
A drinking hall where retired soldiers and mercenaries gather. Informal security, bar brawls, and the occasional job offer for a group needing swords.
A ranger station. They monitor the surrounding wilderness, maintain trails, and keep tabs on beast migrations. In times of crisis they serve as emergency scouts and trackers.
A wilderness post; cities have no wild country inside their reach.
High-level spellcaster residence. Multiple towers possible.
Occasional visits. The smallest spells only.
A resident caster of modest reach. Minor spells only.
Organization of magic users.
Quarter inhabited by arcane practitioners: towers, workshops, libraries, reagent merchants.
Formal institution of arcane learning. Full curriculum, research facilities, visiting scholars.
Spell scrolls for sale. The smallest charm costs what a craftsman earns in a month; a greater working, a merchant’s year.
Permanent teleportation circle. Access is controlled and expensive to maintain. Transformative infrastructure for any settlement lucky enough to have one.
Rare permanent circle. Extremely expensive to construct and maintain. Requires magical expertise beyond typical town resources.
Healer (divine, 1st level)
Basic healing spells. A closed wound costs more than most households see in a month.
Healing in towns runs through the hospitals and the apothecaries.
Formal diplomatic mission from a planar power. Trade, information, occasional intervention.
A rough hall operating under a regional adventurers' charter. Posts bounties, shelters monster hunters, and coordinates local defense where no garrison stands. Common on dangerous frontiers.
A licensed charter hall providing bounties, monster-hunting coordination, and emergency armed response for the surrounding territory. More common in frontier regions.
A chartered hall serving as the primary adventuring hub for the region. Posts contracts, grades monster threats, maintains gear, and coordinates large-scale operations that militia cannot handle.
the senior charter master
the senior charter master
Job board for torchbearers and porters, hired by the session at a day labourer’s wage.
Individual or small groups of professional fighters available for private contracts: bodyguard work, debt enforcement, or quiet removal of problems.
Dungeon delving supply district
Specialized adventuring gear. Warded weapons, silver weapons, etc.
Multiple scholars and researchers.
Fence (word of mouth)
Local contact for moving stolen goods quietly. Operates behind another trade.
Somebody in this settlement buys things without asking where they came from. Everyone knows who. Nobody says it directly.
Stolen goods move through this hamlet quietly. The contact is known by face, not name.
City fencing runs through the black market and the thieves.
Someone here provides cover for people who need to disappear. A barn, a cellar, an arrangement that isn't discussed.
Larger places hide outlaws through bandit ties and smugglers.
One or more households here have ties to bandit groups operating the surrounding roads. Information, shelter, and supply flow both ways.
Towns deal with the road gangs through smugglers and fences.
Goods pass through here to avoid toll roads or customs checkpoints. The hamlet benefits from fees paid in kind.
Goods pass through here to avoid toll roads or customs checkpoints. The village benefits from fees paid in kind.
Illicit goods trade. Tax evasion.
Competing gangs. Turf disputes.
Organized pickpockets and thugs. 10-30 members.
the guildmaster of thieves
Organized crime chapter. 30-100 members.
10,000+ population for viable operation.
A criminal syndicate the city has never rooted out, for fear of the gang war that would follow.
Warehouses, taverns, shops as criminal covers.
Legitimate covers for criminal activity.
An extensive warren of smuggling tunnels beneath the city.
Dug smuggling passages beneath the village.
A dug network of smuggling tunnels and cellars.
Extensive tunnels and catacombs repurposed as criminal and refugee sanctuary.
A loft of message birds kept by people who file no returns. Word arrives unsigned and ahead of the watch. Only a standing criminal organization can protect a loft like this.

A covert guild of brokers who buy and sell knowledge by the piece, grade what they sell, and will manufacture a claim for a patron who pays enough. It sites itself where the talk already is, among the fences, the late houses, and the inns that ask nothing.
Illicit goods trade. Hidden locations.
Permanent underground market: contraband, forged documents, illegal services.
An individual or small cell with no guild behind it. Accepts contracts through criminal intermediaries. Less reliable but deniable.
Professional contract killing. Operates through cutouts, never acknowledged officially.

Targets free persons for fraudulent insertion into slavery through forged provenance documents. Where no lawful market exists to absorb the traffic, it runs its own holding, its own escorts, and its own silence.
Only fires where no legal slave market exists.
Fully clandestine operation moving persons across jurisdictions outside legal channels. Distinct logistics, safe houses, and corrupt border infrastructure.
A resident singer, fiddler, or piper. Plays at festivals and weddings. Also a keeper of local history through song.
Bards, jugglers, acrobats visit at festival time.
Cities keep permanent theaters.
Permanent venues. Professional companies.
High culture. Elite patronage.
Formal musical education. Amphitheater, dormitories.
Dice, cards, simple games of chance.
Dedicated establishments. Some illegal.
Concentrated gaming houses. Play kept honest by compelled truth.
Brothel (red light district)
Legal or tolerated prostitution quarter.
Tolerated or regulated prostitution.
Large organized prostitution quarter.
Illegal or semi-legal combat. Underground locations.
Trains fighters for public spectacle. Recruits from prisoners, debtors, and volunteers. Feeds the arena circuit.
Gladiatorial games or monster fights. Massive scale.
Non-magical 'divination' worked by Deception, for a few coins a reading.
Goods from other planes of existence.
Ancient wyrm living in city.
Animated corpses working. Controversial.
Dream parlors (high magic)
Dream-walking magic sold as experience. Lucid shared dreams, communication.
Airship docking (high magic)
Mooring towers with magical weather protection.
Message network (high magic)
Paired Speaking Stones set in a network. Each station costs as much as a merchant house, and only the richest powers keep one.
The market at {r} is audible before it is visible: a specific mix of voices, animals, and the percussion of commerce that no other combination of sounds quite replicates.
{r}'s market day has the comfortable chaos of something that has been happening in the same place for a long time and has worked out most of its problems.
The road into {r} is thick with carts by mid-morning, all of them heading for the same square, and the traffic tells you where the settlement's heart is before you can see it.
You reach {r} against a tide of people leaving it. The market has ended for the day, and the settlement is exhaling its visitors back onto the roads with their purchases and their news.
Every path into {r} seems to lead to the same place, and you follow the people carrying baskets until it does.
Awnings of every colour cover the middle of {r}, and the buying and selling under them has settled into a steady hum.
Someone on the road into {r} asks whether you are buying or selling, and seems satisfied with either answer.
The smell of the river reaches you before the settlement does: clean water, reeds, the particular mud of a bank that people use every day.
{r} runs along the water the way settlements do when water is the reason they exist: practical, a little chaotic at the waterfront, tidier as you move inland.
The river carries the sounds of {r} to you around the bend before the buildings appear: a mill wheel, the knock of boats against a jetty, someone calling a tally across the water.

{r} has its back to the land and its face to the river; the approach by road brings you in the rear way, past the yards and the drying nets, into a settlement that plainly considers the water its front door.
trade at work: fish
The road into {r} follows the river for the last mile, and the settlement grows along the bank before it grows away from it.
You come into {r} along the riverbank, where steps go down to the water and someone is filling a bucket at the bottom of them.
Trees lean over the river on the way into {r}, and the first houses stand just above the line where the bank turns to mud.
The river bends around {r}, so that you see the settlement twice on the way in: once across the water, and once on arriving.
The harbour at {r} announces itself beyond the last rise: masts above the roofs, gulls wheeling over the quays, and salt bright in the air.
{r} faces the sea as deliberately as a fortress faces its enemy. Warehouses and chandlers crowd the waterfront, with the older streets climbing behind them.
You hear {r}'s harbour before you see it: rigging knocking against masts, dock crews calling cargo tallies, and surf working against the outer wall.
The road into {r} descends toward a forest of masts. Tar, salt, fish, and woodsmoke mark the boundary between the coast and the working port.
The road into {r} comes down to the sea, and the salt reaches you a mile before the first roof does.
{r} sits with its back to the land and its face to the open water, and the wind off the sea carries salt and weed a long way inland.
The last stretch of road into {r} runs beside the sea, and the sound of the surf keeps you company the whole way.
Gulls ride the wind above {r}, and the roofs nearest the water are crusted pale with salt.
Boats ride at their moorings in the harbour below {r}, and the smell of tar and rope comes up the road to meet you.
The cookfire smoke of {r} drifts on the wind in your direction: a hundred fires, each with its own particular fuel, combining into something that smells like inhabited place.
{r} is visible as a smear of smoke on the horizon for a long time before the buildings resolve.
You smell {r} before anything else: woodsmoke and bread and livestock, the layered scent of a place where people have been living close together and cooking the same suppers for generations.
The smoke above {r} stands straight up in the still air, a dozen thin columns that mark the settlement's shape on the sky like a map drawn in grey.
Smoke on the skyline is all you see of {r} for the last hour of the road, and then the roofs are suddenly there.
The wind brings you the smoke of {r} in gusts, now strong, now gone, as the road winds toward it.
Woodsmoke hangs low over {r} in the morning air, and the roofs show through it one at a time as you come closer.
The sound of a hammer on metal reaches you from {r}'s smithing quarter: a craftsperson's rhythm, not a soldier's.
{r} smells of work: sawdust, tallow, the particular sharp smell of a tanner at the edge of town.
{r} announces its trade before its name: the whine of a lathe, the bite of fresh shavings, a workshop door standing open on a scene of unhurried, practised industry.
The approach to {r} is lined with the overflow of its crafts: timber stacked to season, half-finished goods under eaves, the settlement's work spilling out past its walls for want of room inside.
{r} is ordinary in the best sense: a place where people live and work and argue and sleep, which is most of what places are for.
The road into {r} becomes part of the settlement at a point you can't precisely identify. The houses gather around you gradually.
{r} is neither impressive nor disappointing from the approach. It is what it is, which is a working settlement of reasonable size doing reasonable things.
A child runs past you on the road into {r}, chasing something or being chased by something (unclear which). Nobody in the street pays attention.
A child runs past you on the road into {r}, chasing something or being chased by something (unclear which). Nobody else on the road pays attention.
A child runs past you on the road into {name}, chasing something or being chased by something (unclear which). Nobody in the street pays attention.
A merchant argues with a carter on the road into {r} about the size of a load. Nobody else pays them any attention. This is clearly a daily occurrence.
The first person you meet on the road into {r} wants to know your business, and the second already knows it.
The first building you pass on the way into {r} is somebody's house, and so is the second, and so, it turns out, is most of the rest.
A dog trots out to look you over on the road into {r}, decides you are of no interest, and trots back.
Washing hangs in the yards along the road into {r}, and someone calls a greeting from behind it without looking to see who you are.
A cart has stopped half across the road into {r} while its driver talks to someone over a fence, and nobody minds going round it.
{r} does not announce itself: the road simply gathers more doors, then a well, and then you are in it.
{r} has no one thing to look at as you come in, only a great many small ones: a mended fence, a painted door, a bench beside a house.

The gates of {r} are closed. There are people on the walls. This is not the relaxed watch of a settlement going about its day. These are people watching the treeline. A face shows at the grille of the small side gate, sees your group, and is gone.

{r}'s gates are shut and barred. The guards on them are professional about it, which makes it worse: nobody comes near without being challenged, and nothing is let through. Professional means they expect this to last.

From outside, {r} still seems itself: smoke from cookfires, a murmur from the square. It is the gate that gives it away: shut fast, the guards' faces set, their talk stopping dead when strangers come in sight.

The approach to {r} is quieter than it should be for a settlement this size. The outlying farms are empty. The road has not been maintained recently. The settlement itself is intact, but everything around it has been abandoned to the walls.
The fields around {r} were harvested early and badly: stubble cut in haste, carts gone. Whatever the walls are waiting for, the granaries inside are already keeping its schedule.
A thrown stone sits half-buried a hundred paces short of {r}'s wall, left where it landed. Nobody has hauled it away. There are fresher things to attend to.
{n} has drawn in on itself. Every family from the outlying fields is sleeping under a neighbour's roof, the livestock are penned between the houses, and someone is always watching the treeline.
There are campfires on the hill above {n}, and they are not {n}'s. The people inside keep their own fires low and their voices lower, and they count the strangers' fires every night.
Carts and timber block the lanes into {n}, piled in a hurry and manned around the clock. The faces behind them are farmers' faces, and none of them has slept.

{r} looks prosperous in the merchant quarter: new paint, loaded carts, a market stall with produce. It is only when you walk further in that the other version of the settlement appears: shuttered houses, people sitting on doorsteps with no particular purpose.
{r} is functional. The market is open, the streets are swept, the guards are at their posts. Something is wrong anyway. It takes a moment to identify: there are no children playing in the street.

The queue at the granary gate is the first thing you see in {r}. Not a market queue, not a water queue: the organised, patient, daily queue of people who are waiting to receive what they are owed and are not certain they will receive it.

{r} is orderly in the way that a settlement is orderly when order is being enforced. The streets are clear. The rationing markers are painted on the doors. A guard patrol passes and everyone steps aside.
The dogs of {r} are gone. It takes a while to notice and longer to stop noticing, and nobody in the settlement will discuss it with a stranger.

Prices chalked outside {r}'s market gate have been rubbed out and rewritten so often the board has gone grey. The numbers on it now are polite fictions; the real trading happens in back rooms, in kind.
The smoke from {n}'s chimneys is thin. People here look at your pack before they look at your face, and then look away, ashamed of having looked.
{r} is quiet in the way a hungry settlement is quiet. The rationing markers are painted on the doors, and people keep to their own thresholds.

{name} is orderly in the way that a settlement is orderly when order is being enforced. The streets are clear. The rationing markers are painted on the doors. A guard patrol passes and everyone steps aside.

The flags above {r}'s gatehouse are not the settlement's own. Two soldiers at the gate. Their uniform is not local. They look at your papers with the particular expression of people who have been told to look at papers.

{r} looks normal from the approach. It is only at the gate that the nature of normal becomes apparent: the guard asks where you are from, writes it down, and asks how long you intend to stay. This is not the usual question.
The approach to {r} looks like any other settlement. There is graffiti on the wall near the gate that someone has attempted to scrub off. The symbol is still readable.

{r} is going about its business. The market is open, the streets are orderly, the gates are attended by soldiers whose armour is not local. Everyone is doing what they are supposed to be doing, which is the point.
{r}'s notices are posted in two languages now, the local one second. The new lettering is neat, official, and on every door that matters, which is how you learn the occupation intends to stay.
At {r}'s gate the queue divides in two: residents with papers, and everyone else. The residents' line is longer and moves slower, and no one in it complains where the soldiers can hear.
Strangers in foreign colours stand about in the middle of {n}, and the locals walk around them as if they were furniture nobody wanted.
{r} has two gates. The eastern one is controlled by one power, the western by another. You can tell by the pennants. The road you are on leads to the eastern gate.
The gate guard at {r} asks where you intend to stay: which inn, which district. The answer apparently matters. They note it and say nothing further.

The road into {r} has been marked. Symbols painted on fence posts and milestone stones: the same symbol, repeated, belonging to one power or another. Someone has been doing this recently; the paint is fresh.

{r} is quieter than it should be. Not the quiet of a sleeping town or a working one: the particular quiet of a place where people have learned to be careful about what they say in earshot of strangers.

Two tax collectors work {r}'s market: different sashes, different ledgers, studiously ignoring one another. Traders pay one, or the other, or both, according to calculations a visitor is not equipped to make.
The council hall of {r} is dark; the business of governing has moved to two different taverns at opposite ends of town. Which one you drink in has become a declaration.

{r} is in reasonable shape. The walls are standing, the market is functioning, the main street is paved. The paving needs repair. The wall has a section of new brick that doesn't quite match the old. The repairs that needed doing five years ago are still waiting.
A building near the gate has a new sign, freshly painted with the name of an outside creditor. The creditor has opened an office here, and the locals walk past it without looking in.
{r} gets by. The market is busy enough, the streets clean enough and the civic buildings kept up just enough, and nothing more is being spent.
The merchant district of {r} looks prosperous. The rest of the settlement, visible further in, looks like it has been waiting for the merchant district's prosperity to reach it for some years.

The finest building in {r} is new, stone-built, and belongs to nobody local: a counting house, its brass plate polished daily by a clerk who arrived with the ledgers. It is what everything else in town is working to pay for.

{r} holds a market day that has quietly become a collection day: the stalls pay their pitch fees to a factor before they sell a thing, and the factor's book has more names in it than the market has stalls.
The best-kept street of {r} looks prosperous. The rest of the settlement, visible further in, looks like it has been waiting for that street's prosperity to reach it for some years.
The merchant district of {name} looks prosperous. The rest of the settlement, visible further in, looks like it has been waiting for the merchant district's prosperity to reach it for some years.
The guard at {r}'s gate is polite, thorough, and writes down more than guards usually write down. You are asked your business three times, by three different people, in the space of five minutes.
Something has happened in {r} lately. Conversations drop to a murmur as you pass, and people watch the street from their doorways.

There are notices posted at the gate of {r}. You take a moment to read one: it is asking for information about a specific event, with a contact at the council offices. The date on the notice is recent.
{r} looks ordinary from the approach. It is only in the expressions of the people at the gate (watchful in a specific, tired way) that something registers.
{r} has new locks. You can see the bright hasps on doors and shutters as you walk in: ironmongery bought all at once, recently, by people who used not to need it.

Conversation in {r}'s common room stops at the creak of the door-hinge, resumes a beat later, carefully general. Whatever happened here, everyone has already said everything they intend to say about it.
{r} looks exactly like it should. The gate is attended, the market sounds busy, there is nothing remarkable about the approach. Everything is as it should be.
The approach to {r} is unremarkable in every respect. Gate, road, market noise, smoke, the usual questions from the guard. Nothing to note.
{r} looks normal. There is a moment at the gate (a guard glancing at another guard after you answer a question) that is probably nothing.
{r} is functioning well. Clean streets, busy market, maintained walls. If you were looking for problems, you would not find them from the outside.
Nothing in {r} is out of place. The watch changes on the hour, the market closes at dusk, the innkeeper remembers your name on the second morning. It is all exactly as a well-run town should be.
{r} welcomes travellers with practised ease: a good inn, fair prices, incurious guards. A week later you would struggle to say why the ease sat strangely. It was practised.
{n} is friendly. Everyone you meet is helpful, and everyone you meet asks one question more than they need to: where you are going next, and who you know there.
{n} runs smoothly, almost too smoothly. Quarrels that should be loud are settled quietly and fast, and nobody can quite tell you who settled them.
In {n} the same stranger seems to turn up wherever you go: at the well, on the road, at the edge of every conversation. He never says much. He never needs to.

The approach to {r} is interrupted by a checkpoint a quarter mile from the gates: a temporary structure, manned by people wearing cloth over their faces. They want to know where you came from and when.

{r}'s gate is open, the market is running, and there are people in the street. People are giving each other slightly more space than usual. A cart passes with barrels marked with an unfamiliar symbol. You have seen that symbol once before, on a quarantine notice.
Near the gate of {r} there is a temporary shelter: a healer's station, by the look of it, with two attendants and a queue. The queue is not yet long. That is either good or early.

Some of {r}'s market stalls are closed. Not all, not most, but several, in a pattern that isn't about the day of the week. The ones that are open are busy; the ones that are closed have been for a while.
{r}'s gate stands open, but the gatekeeper waves you through from a distance, and the well just inside has been roped off under a painted sign too weathered to read from horseback.
Smoke rises from {r} at midday: not cookfires but something being burned deliberately, bedding or clothes, in a yard behind the healer's house. The street watches it burn and says nothing.
{n} smells of vinegar and woodsmoke. Doors that should be open are shut, and the people who do come out keep a careful distance from one another, and from you.
There are two sets of pennants above {r}'s main gate: different colours, same height. Someone made a decision to hang them both and has committed to maintaining the ambiguity.
{r} has the specific quality of a settlement waiting for news. People are going about their business, but there is a particular alertness to the street: people checking who is talking to whom.

The road into {r} has been busy recently. You can tell by the wheel ruts, the quality of the mud, the number of horses at the inn you pass on the approach. Something is happening that requires people to arrive quickly.
{r} functions, after a fashion. The market is open, the gates are attended. The flagpole above the council building is empty. Someone removed the standard and hasn't replaced it yet.
Building has stopped mid-job across {r}; scaffolding stands empty on dressed stone. Work that fine waits on a patron, and the town is not currently sure who that is.
In {r}'s taproom the toast is to "the settlement": a formulation everyone has adopted at once, smooth as furniture, since naming anyone more specific has become a wager.
{r} is more fortified than its size suggests. The walls are new (or newly repaired), the mortar still pale. There are more torches at the gate than a settlement like this would normally need.

The farms outside {r} are partially abandoned. You count three sets of buildings that have not been worked recently: the fields untended, the doors standing open. The settlement's wall is a quarter mile closer than it would have been three months ago.
{r}'s gate is attended by its usual guards and, less usually, by several people in road-worn equipment who are clearly not local and clearly not merchants. The settlement is paying for help.

{r} is going about its business, but the business includes people you wouldn't normally see on a market day: hunters checking arrows, a blacksmith working past dark, a group of militia running a drill in the square visible from the gate.
The road into {r} runs its last mile between new watchtowers: timber, hasty, manned. Whatever they watch for, the fields between them have been let go to seed.
{r} buys arrows. The fletcher's is the busiest shop in the settlement, and the militia board outside the gate lists a standing bounty in terms that carefully avoid naming what it is for.
{n} keeps its doors barred in daylight. Claw marks score the timber of the outermost houses, old ones and new ones, and the newest have not yet weathered.
Every household in {n} keeps a spear by the door, and the children know which way to run. Nobody says what they would be running from. They say it is the woods.
Fresh earth marks a row of graves at the edge of {n}, all dug in the same week. The people who dug them still glance at the treeline while they work.

The approach to {r} is ordinary until you notice what is missing: no toll-keeper at the gate, no one collecting the road tax a settlement this size always collects. The guards are present, but they are watching the town, not the road.

{r}'s gate stands open and unmanned. Further in, two different sets of notices are posted on the same wall: one in the formal hand of the authorities, one hand-lettered and torn at the corner. Someone tears down the second kind. Someone keeps putting them back.

There are soldiers on {r}'s streets, but they move in pairs and do not linger. The people watch them pass with the particular blankness of a place that has already decided which side it is on and is waiting to be asked.

{r} looks governed, and is not, quite. The market runs, the watch patrols, the council building is occupied. But the orders that leave that building are not always the orders that get followed, and everyone in the street knows which is which.
The garrison of {r} patrols in daylight only, and along routes a stranger could predict by the third day. After dark the town belongs to whoever it belongs to.
Someone has been chalking a sign on {r}'s walls faster than the watch can scrub it. By now the scrubbed patches themselves mark every corner. The censorship has become the graffiti.
Slogans have been scratched into the doors of {n} overnight and half scrubbed away by morning. People read them on the way past without stopping, which is how you know they agree.

The road into {r} is crowded: not with merchants but with families, carts piled with household goods, people who are clearly not from here and clearly not passing through. The gate guard has stopped checking papers. There are too many.

{r} has grown a second settlement outside its walls: tents and lean-tos and cookfires on the ground that used to be common pasture. The people there watch you approach with the wariness of those who arrived too late to get inside.

Half of {r} seems to have arrived this year. You pass loaded wagons on the road heading in, and inside the walls every spare room has a family in it. Those who were here first have the look of people deciding how much more they can give.

{r}'s market speaks three languages you can pick out and more you cannot. The old families and the newcomers trade at the same stalls and do not quite look at each other. Everyone is doing business. No one is comfortable.
The road to {r} has acquired a verge of graves: recent, orderly, unmarked but tended. People arrived here in numbers, and not all of them finished the journey.
{r}'s smithy has a queue for wheel-rims and none for ploughshares. A town where the carts outnumber the fields is a town still filling with people who came here with everything they own.

The road to {r} has been rutted deep by heavy wagons moving in one direction: toward the settlement loaded, away from it loaded differently. At the gate a clerk with an army seal records what comes and goes. This is a war's traffic, not trade's.

{r}'s young men are not in {r}. You notice it at the gate and it holds true inside: the people working the stalls and the fields are the old, the very young, and the women. A recruiting notice is nailed to the gatepost, its edges soft with weather.

There are more soldiers than citizens visible on {r}'s main street, and the citizens are the ones stepping aside. A requisition column is being loaded in the square: grain, cloth, iron, and the settlement's own carts to carry it away.
{r} is busy in a way that feels wrong. The forge fires burn past dark, the coin is moving, and all of it points one direction, toward a war that is not fought here but is paid for here.
{r}'s noticeboard is a wall of requisition orders, each stamped, each superseding the last. At its foot, a smaller paper, hand-lettered: prayers offered nightly, all welcome.
The horses in {r}'s paddocks are old, or lame, or foals. Every sound animal of working age has a receipt where it used to be, and the receipts do not say when the army returns them.

{r} is busy in a way that feels wrong for a place this poor. The forge fires burn past dark, but the coin they earn leaves with the carts, and all of it points one direction, toward a war that is not fought here but is paid for here.
{name} is busy in a way that feels wrong. The forge fires burn past dark, the coin is moving, and all of it points one direction, toward a war that is not fought here but is paid for here.

Two temples face each other across {r}'s central square, and only one has a queue. The other's doors are open but its steps are swept too clean, walked on too little. Something has moved from one building to the other, and it was not only worshippers.

The shrine at {r}'s gate has been recently altered: one symbol chiselled away, another set in its place, the old outline still faintly visible beneath the new. Someone did this carefully. Someone else has been scratching at the replacement.

{r} is observing a holy day, and you cannot tell which one. Some shops are shut and draped; others are pointedly open. Two processions are forming at opposite ends of the settlement, and the people watching each are counting who watches the other.
The bells of {r} ring twice for every hour: one set of chimes, then another from a different quarter, a beat later and out of tune. Nobody in the street looks up.
The busiest work in {r} is on its holy symbols: one set coming down, another going up, and the same three workmen paid for both. They no longer joke about it.

The dead of {r} are buried in two rows now, the old faith's and the new, and the town's grief is learning to sort itself accordingly. Whoever digs the graves digs both, and is the most carefully neutral soul alive.

{r}'s gates are shut in daylight, which is wrong for a settlement of its size. There is smoke inside: not cookfire smoke, too much and too dark. On the wall, the guards face inward, toward their own streets, not out toward you.

The approach to {r} is blocked by a hasty checkpoint: overturned carts, armed men who are not the regular watch, a hard question about your business before you are allowed within sight of the gate. Whatever is happening inside, they have decided strangers are a risk.

{r} is quiet in the way a held breath is quiet. The slave market at its heart (you can see the empty auction platform from the gate) stands deserted, ringed by guards. The chains are still there. The people who wore them are not.

There are bodies being carried through {r}'s streets under cloth, and the people carrying them are not mourners but labourers doing grim, fast work. The rising that did this is not finished; you can hear it, somewhere in the lower districts, still going on.
One building in {r} is shuttered and scorched, the only burned one in sight, which tells you the fire was a statement, not an accident.
{r}'s field hands work without overseers today, or the overseers have dressed like the hands. From the road you cannot tell which, and that is the whole story of the settlement this season.
Whatever the settlement was built for, it is under siege now, and nothing else matters until the siege is broken.
Whatever the site was chosen for matters little to the people now deciding whether its walls can hold.
These walls were built in case they were ever needed. They are needed now.
This place has fed its people well enough in other years. Now its food is failing and families are going hungry.
Whatever fed the settlement in other years has failed it this year, and its children are going hungry.
The country around the settlement looks the same as ever, but the food has come in short, and the winter ahead will be hard.
The settlement's own rulers used to give the orders. Now foreign officers give them, and those rulers answer to them.
Nobody here chose the people who rule it now, and they answer to someone far away.
The settlement always made its own decisions, or believed it did. Under occupation, it no longer does.
The people of the settlement no longer agree on what it is for, and nobody expects them to agree again soon.
Its people work as hard as they ever did, but no longer agree on where the settlement is going.
Every power here tells the settlement's story its own way, and the settlement has split along those lines.
The first settlers built something worth having. Their descendants have borrowed against it until the settlement owes more than it owns.
Each generation since the founding has borrowed a little more against what the founders left. Now the lenders want it back.
What the founders built was solid enough to borrow against, and it has been, again and again; the lenders now own much of it.
The settlement runs on trust between its households, and one of its own has just broken that trust.
Life here rests on promises kept between neighbours, and someone inside has just broken one.
People here trusted each other without thinking about it. Someone inside has just made them think about it.
The settlement has always trusted familiar faces, and it still does. Someone living here now is using that trust to hide.
A place this size still trusts faces it knows, and one of those faces is not what it seems.
The settlement still believes it knows who lives inside its walls. That is how someone who does not belong goes unnoticed.
The sickness came in the way everything else here comes in: from outside, and before anyone thought to stop it.
Whatever made this a good place to settle, the sickness found its way here all the same.
The sickness reached it as easily as news does, and faster than anyone could shut a door against it.
The founding generation is gone, and nobody agrees who should lead now.
The founders settled many things but never who would rule after them. Now the seat is empty, and rivals are fighting over it.
Every office here was handed down from the founders, and now nobody can agree who it passes to.
The founders knew this ground was dangerous and settled anyway. Now the danger has come back to the fields.
The first settlers judged this land worth its dangers. With something coming out of the wild again, people are asking whether they were right.
The founders cleared this land from the wild. Now something from the wild is coming back for it.
The settlement was founded on an authority its people once accepted. That acceptance has been withdrawn, and no one has agreed on what should replace it.
The founders assumed the settlement could always be governed. Now some of its own people are refusing to be.
The rules the founders set have outlived the reasons for them, and people have stopped obeying.
The settlement was never built for this many. Now newcomers crowd in, and half the faces are strangers.
The settlement was laid out for the people it used to hold. Its houses and its water were never meant for this many.
The settlement once knew the faces inside its walls. Now it does not: too many have arrived too fast.
The settlement grew up in quieter years. Now it feeds and arms a war.
Whatever the settlement was built for, it is paying for a war now, and the bill grows every season.
Now the army takes what the settlement used to sell, and pays what the army thinks fair.
The founding was blessed under a faith that is no longer ascendant here. The oaths and endowments made in its name are now contested ground.
The first stones were laid with prayers the settlement no longer says, and the land and duties promised in them are now in dispute.
The settlement was consecrated in a faith now out of favour, and nobody agrees what that old blessing still binds them to.
The settlement ran on slaves it never counted as its own people. Now they have risen.
For years this place has run on enslaved hands. Those hands have turned against it.
Its masters worked it with slaves and kept the profits. The slaves have risen, and they mean to take back what was taken from them.

Was present at (and did nothing to prevent) an atrocity that is now history
